title: Hidden Figures
learn: NASA computing, orbital mathematics, how unrecognized work makes exploration possible
knowledge: Space race, segregation, women in STEM, NASA Langley
questions: Why do you think Katherine kept pushing forward when the room was not built for her?
What is the difference between being allowed in a room and being respected in it?
Who are the 'hidden figures' in work you see around you?
activity: Look up how long sunlight takes to reach Earth, then how long a radio signal takes to reach the Moon. Sketch the two distances.
parent: Strong first title for barriers and persistence. Pause for the bathroom-run scene and ask what the rule was really protecting.
content: Historical racism, segregated facilities, workplace sexism; no graphic violence. Some period tension.

title: Inside Out
learn: Named emotions, memory, why sadness is useful, how a move can scramble identity
knowledge: Basic psychology of feelings; family relocation
questions: When did Sadness help Riley more than Joy did?
What would happen if one emotion ran the whole console?
Which of Riley's islands feels most like you right now?
activity: Draw a five-emotion console for a real day this week. Label one memory that changed color after you talked about it.
parent: Best on-ramp to feeling words. Watch for kids who treat Joy as the 'correct' emotion — the film argues otherwise.
content: Anxiety and sadness portrayed vividly; brief implied depression. No frightening villains.

title: Coco
learn: Family memory, artistic vocation, how culture keeps people present after death
qualities: Empathy, courage, respect for elders, creative grit
knowledge: Día de los Muertos, Mexican family tradition, ofrenda practice
questions: Why does Miguel's family ban music if music is how they remember?
What does it mean that being forgotten is the second death?
Who would you put on an ofrenda and why?
activity: Make a small ofrenda or memory table for someone you love: photo, favorite food, one object, one story told out loud.
parent: Death is central but treated as continuation through memory. Good for families processing loss if you preview first.
content: Themes of death and being forgotten; mild action. Culturally specific and worth naming as tradition, not costume.

title: Encanto
learn: Family roles, giftedness vs. worth, what happens when a house (or family) cracks
knowledge: Colombian-inspired culture, intergenerational family systems
questions: What is Bruno's real 'gift' besides seeing the future?
Which family member is carrying a job that does not fit them?
What would your family miracle be, and what would it cost?
activity: Each person writes a hidden pressure they carry on a card. Trade and invent a kind sentence the family could say instead of 'we don't talk about it.'
parent: Use for perfectionism and sibling comparison. Mirabel having no gift is the point, not a problem to fix.
content: Family tension, implied trauma in Abuela's past; no on-screen violence. Songs carry the argument.

title: Moana
learn: Wayfinding, stewardship of the ocean, identity beyond a parent's fear
knowledge: Pacific voyaging culture, ecological imbalance as story metaphor
questions: Why does Tala push Moana toward the reef when her father forbids it?
Is Maui a hero, a cautionary tale, or both?
What does 'know who you are' mean after the journey, not before?
activity: Try a simple navigation challenge: cross a park or block using only landmarks and the sun, no phone.
parent: Strong for kids who need permission to try a hard thing. Separate Polynesian inspiration from 'generic island movie.'
content: Mild peril at sea, lava being, comic sidekick. Some kids find Te Kā intense; sit close.

title: How to Train Your Dragon
learn: Enemies can be misunderstood; invention plus kindness changes a culture
qualities: Empathy, courage, creative thinking, moral independence
knowledge: Prejudice as inherited story; prosthetic/adaptive design (Hiccup's foot, Toothless's tail)
questions: What did Hiccup notice that the other Vikings refused to look at?
Why is it harder to change your father's mind than to fight a dragon?
Where do we still tell 'they are all dangerous' stories?
activity: Design a helpful prosthetic or tool for an animal or person on paper. Label the problem it solves.
parent: Excellent prejudice conversation without a lecture. The night-fury scene is the whole thesis: look closer.
content: Battle sequences, parental injury, a prosthetic outcome. Intensity rises in the nest battle.

title: Wonder
learn: Perspective-taking, friendship under social pressure, how kindness is a practice
knowledge: Facial difference, school inclusion, family stress around medical care
questions: Why does the film keep switching whose eyes we see through?
When is 'being nice' not the same as being a friend?
What would you want classmates to do on a first day like Auggie's?
activity: Write the same cafeteria scene from three seats: Auggie, Jack, Via. Read them aloud and mark what each person cannot see.
parent: Preview if your child has been bullied or has a visible difference. The precepts make a good week-long dinner ritual.
content: Bullying, social exclusion, medical history. Not graphic; emotionally heavy for sensitive 8–9 year olds.

title: October Sky
learn: Amateur rocketry, scientific method through failure, leaving a town without rejecting it
knowledge: Sputnik era, coal-town economics, contest science
questions: Why does Homer keep launching after the rockets fail in public?
What does his father fear losing if Homer leaves the mine?
Who is the most important teacher in the film who is not in a classroom?
activity: Build and test a bottle rocket or paper rocket. Log three failures and what you changed after each.
parent: Quiet, true-story energy. Good for kids who think science is only for 'geniuses already ahead.'
content: Mine disaster tension, father-son conflict, period smoking. No sensational violence.

title: Apollo 13
learn: Engineering under constraint, teamwork on the ground matching courage in the capsule
knowledge: Apollo program, orbital mechanics at a story level, Mission Control culture
questions: Why is 'failure is not an option' a team sentence, not a hero sentence?
Which fix in the film is the most creative use of leftover parts?
How do the families on the ground practice courage differently from the crew?
activity: Give the family a 'square peg, round hole' challenge: solve a household problem using only items from one drawer.
parent: Long but gripping. You can watch in two nights. Emphasize the ground crew as co-protagonists.
content: Sustained peril, oxygen crisis, brief tempers. Based on real events; some kids ask if the crew dies — tell them no before you start if needed.

title: WALL-E
learn: Robotics and automation, consumer waste, what humans forget how to do
knowledge: Environmental collapse as cautionary future; plant life as a restart signal
questions: What does WALL-E know how to do that the people on the ship have forgotten?
Why is a single plant more important than all the ads?
If a robot can be lonely, what is the film saying about attention?
activity: Do a home 'trash audit' for one day. Sort landfill / recycle / compost and set one reduction goal for the week.
parent: Almost silent first act is a gift: ask kids to narrate what WALL-E wants before EVE arrives.
content: Bleak empty Earth may unsettle younger children. Comic tone returns; no gore.

title: Big Hero 6
learn: Robotics, prototyping, grief redirected into purpose rather than revenge
knowledge: Applied engineering, superhero ethics, sibling loss
questions: When does Hiro stop building to hurt and start building to help?
What is Baymax's actual job description, and why does that matter in a fight?
Which teammate's 'soft' skill saves the mission?
activity: Invent a helper robot on paper: one job, three sensors, one safety rule it must never break.
parent: The death is early and clear. Pause. Baymax's care protocol is the moral center — name it.
content: Sibling death, fire, action violence. Tone is adventurous after the funeral; still a real loss.

title: The Wild Robot
learn: Adaptation, parenting without a manual, ecosystems as networks not scenery
knowledge: Migration, predator-prey, what 'programmed' vs. 'chosen' might mean
questions: When does Roz stop being a machine that washes ashore and start being a mother?
Why do the animals need her to change more than they need her to stay efficient?
What rule would you keep if you were stranded and had to belong?
activity: Map a backyard or park food web with at least eight species. Add one 'Roz' — an outsider who changes the map.
parent: Gentle face, real stakes. Excellent for kids who intellectualize feelings; the robot learns them in public.
content: Animal peril and death in the cycle of nature; storms; mild action. Sad in places, not cruel.

title: Ratatouille
learn: Craft takes taste plus practice; gatekeeping in art; collaboration across status lines
knowledge: French kitchen brigade, food criticism, who gets to be called an artist
questions: Is Linguini the cook, the partner, or the front?
Why does Ego's review matter more than the crowd's applause?
What talent in your house is hiding in the 'wrong' body or room?
activity: Cook one simple dish together from scratch. Plate it as if a critic is coming, then write a four-sentence review that is specific, not just 'yummy.'
parent: Use for kids who think talent is magic. Gusteau's line is the whole site in one sentence: anyone can cook.
content: Comic chase peril, health-inspector tension, a gunshot scare at the start for some kids. Generally gentle.

title: Paddington 2
learn: Manners as social technology, how one kind person rearranges a neighborhood
knowledge: London community life, prisons as places that can still hold humor and reform (story-level)
questions: What does Paddington do that makes hard people softer?
Is 'if we are kind and polite the world will be right' always true? When is it still worth trying?
Who in the film needs a second chance more than a punishment?
activity: Write and deliver one useful thank-you (not a compliment) to someone who keeps your daily life running.
parent: The rare film that teaches manners without nagging. Pop-up book sequence is a creativity master class.
content: Wrongful imprisonment, mild villainy, comic danger. Very safe emotionally for most 6+.

title: Zootopia
learn: Bias can hide inside people who think they are the good guys; cities are systems
knowledge: Stereotypes, policing and trust, urban design as metaphor
questions: When does Judy catch herself doing the thing she hates?
Why is 'predator' a dangerous nickname even when it started as biology?
What stereotype do people put on you, and what do they miss?
activity: Invent two animals and write the rumor about each. Then write one fact that makes the rumor fall apart.
parent: Do not skip the Judy-Nick sidewalk scene. That is the learning. The night howler plot is just the vehicle.
content: Prejudice themes, mild noir menace, a sloth joke that runs long. Some intense predator-prey framing for younger kids.

title: Soul
learn: Purpose vs. spark; a life is more than the job you wanted
qualities: Curiosity, presence, humility, creative love of craft
knowledge: Jazz as practice, philosophy of vocation at kid-accessible level
questions: What is the difference between Joe's 'purpose' and 22's 'spark'?
When is ambition a gift and when is it a trap?
What ordinary thing in your day would a soul who has never lived find amazing?
activity: Each person lists four 'spark' moments from an ordinary day (not achievements). Put them on the fridge for a week.
parent: More philosophical than most Pixar. Best at 10+ unless you like pausing to translate. Jazz scenes reward a short music detour.
content: Afterlife abstraction, a character in a hospital, existential dread played gently. Not scary; can feel big.

title: The Mitchells vs. the Machines
learn: Family as mismatched operating systems; screens as connection and capture
qualities: Creativity, flexibility, family loyalty, media literacy
knowledge: AI hype as comedy; how algorithms flatten people into types
questions: What does Katie make that a machine cannot rank?
Why does the dad's 'plan' keep failing his actual kids?
When does a phone help this family, and when does it steal them?
activity: Shoot a 60-second family movie with phones in a drawer except the camera. Credits required.
parent: Loud and dense visually. Great for creative kids who feel unseen by practical parents — and the reverse.
content: Robot apocalypse comedy, mild peril, family yelling. Overstimulating for some; harmless morally.

title: Akeelah and the Bee
learn: Language as power, community coaching, excellence without abandoning home
knowledge: Scripps-style spelling, South L.A. community, etymology as a tool
questions: Why is Akeelah afraid to look like she cares?
What does Dr. Larabee mean by 'our language'?
Who in your life would show up if you trained for something hard?
activity: Pick five words. Find root + language of origin + one sentence you would actually use. Hold a five-word family bee.
parent: Old-fashioned in the best way. Affirms neighborhood pride and high standards in the same breath.
content: Grief (father's death in backstory), class tension, pressure. No violence of note.

title: Remember the Titans
learn: Integration is work, not a speech; teams can lead towns or copy them
knowledge: Virginia school integration era, football as civic stage
questions: What changes first — the locker room or the town?
When does Boone's toughness help, and when does Yoast's gentleness?
Who on the team is brave off the field?
activity: Choose a group you belong to. Write one rule that would make a newcomer feel the group is actually shared.
parent: Sports movie that earns its history. Some language and racial slurs are period-accurate; preview and plan to pause.
content: Racist language and threats, injury, a car accident. PG but emotionally adult in places.

title: The Boy Who Harnessed the Wind
learn: Practical physics, libraries as infrastructure, engineering as family survival
qualities: Ingenuity, persistence, filial respect, civic courage
knowledge: Malawi famine context, wind energy basics, education access
questions: Why is the library more important than the broken pump at first?
What does William have to risk in his father's eyes to try the mill?
How is this different from a 'gifted kid' movie set in a lab?
activity: Build a pinwheel or small wind toy and test it in three places. Which location wins and why?
parent: Heavier than most on this list (hunger, political violence at a distance). Worth it for 11+ with context. True story.
content: Famine, poverty, brief unrest. PG-13 for thematic intensity more than images. Watch first if your child is sensitive to hunger stories.

title: Queen of Katwe
learn: Chess as thinking sport, talent plus transport plus a coach
qualities: Focus, confidence, family loyalty, strategic patience
knowledge: Kampala / Katwe life, competitive chess, what 'opportunity' actually costs a family
questions: What does Phiona see on the board that she also needs off the board?
Why is leaving for a tournament a family decision, not just hers?
Who wins if she wins — only Phiona?
activity: Learn and play three games of chess (or checkers). After each, name one mistake you will not repeat.
parent: Disney drama with real texture. Good counterweight to 'pull yourself up' myths — community is the engine.
content: Poverty, a missing father, mild peril in the slum setting. No graphic content.

title: Holes
learn: Cause and effect across generations, friendship as survival, justice delayed
knowledge: American tall-tale structure, desert ecology lite, juvenile detention critique (story-level)
questions: What 'curse' is actually a chain of human choices?
Why does Zero matter more than the treasure?
Where is an adult using kids to do dirty work?
activity: Draw the story as a family tree of cause and effect: one injustice leading to the next, then the repair.
parent: Funny and dark. Pause on Camp Green Lake's rules — kids recognize unfair systems fast if you let them.
content: Cruel adults, forced labor, historical racism in flashbacks, implied danger. PG with bite.

title: Finding Nemo
learn: Overprotection vs. trust, ocean habitats, asking for help
knowledge: Coral reef, currents, fish adaptations (popular-science level)
questions: What is Marlin afraid of that is no longer happening?
How does Dory's way of thinking save them?
When should a parent let a child take a risk?
activity: Pick three ocean animals from the film and find one true fact and one movie invention about each.
parent: Opening is harsher than people remember. You can start after it for younger kids and still keep the theme.
content: Predator attacks, separation trauma at the start, comic peril after. G-rated but the first minutes sting.

title: Kiki's Delivery Service
learn: Independence, creative burnout, finding work that fits a gift
knowledge: Coming-of-age work life; artist block as a real event
questions: Why does Kiki lose her magic when she starts comparing herself?
What does the baker give her that is not money?
What would 'open a small business at 13' teach you that school does not?
activity: Offer one real helpful service this week (walk, bake, organize, draw). Charge nothing; write what was hard besides the task.
parent: The quietest courage film on the list. Ideal for kids entering a new school or sport.
content: Very gentle. A flying scare or two. No villains.

title: My Neighbor Totoro
learn: Attention to ordinary nature, waiting, sibling care while adults are stretched
knowledge: Japanese countryside living, soot sprites as household folklore
questions: What do the girls notice because they are not in a hurry?
Why doesn't the film explain Totoro?
How do Mei and Satsuki take care of each other when Mother is away?
activity: Take a 20-minute 'noticing walk.' Each person must bring back three things they never named before.
parent: Mother's illness is background, not a twist. If a parent is sick in real life, preview. Otherwise it is comfort cinema.
content: Hospital visits, a lost-child scare that resolves. No antagonists.

title: Hugo
learn: Early cinema history, clocks and automata, repairing people by repairing things
knowledge: Georges Méliès, birth of movie magic, 1930s Paris station life
questions: Why does Papa Georges hide the part of himself that made films?
What is the difference between stealing a machine and stealing a life?
How is a movie like a clock?
activity: Watch one very short early film (Méliès' Trip to the Moon is ideal). List three tricks that still show up in movies today.
parent: A love letter to movies themselves — meta in a useful way for this site. Long for some 8-year-olds; an intermission works.
content: Orphanhood, a station inspector who looks scarier than he is, brief war injury backstory.

title: Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse
learn: Style as meaning, multiple versions of a person, stepping up without being 'the' chosen one first
qualities: Courage, originality, responsibility, humor under pressure
knowledge: Comic-book visual language; Brooklyn family life
questions: Why does Miles's world look different from Peter's?
What does 'anyone can wear the mask' add to 'with great power'?
When does Miles stop imitating and start inventing?
activity: Draw the same hero three ways (stick, realistic, wild). Write one sentence each version would say about fear.
parent: Form is content: the look teaches creative confidence. Action is punchy; fine for most 10+.
content: Comic-book fights, a parent in danger, some menace. PG action, not grim.

title: The Iron Giant
learn: You are what you choose, not what you were built for; fear makes bad policy
knowledge: 1950s Cold War mood, weapons panic as social story
questions: Who decides what the Giant is — the government, Hogarth, or the Giant?
Why is 'Superman' a better instruction than 'weapon'?
What fear in the town looks like a fact but is actually a story?
activity: Write two headlines about the same event: one from fear, one from curiosity. Discuss which one you would click and why.
parent: Short, perfect, and the ending needs a talk. Kids often ask if the Giant dies. Stay for that conversation.
content: Military force, a sacrificial ending, guns. Emotionally larger than its runtime.

title: Luca
learn: Friendship as bravery, hiding vs. belonging, curiosity about the 'other side'
knowledge: Italian coastal town life; difference as metaphor (read it as you need)
questions: What is Luca not allowed to be curious about, and who made that rule?
When does hiding protect him, and when does it shrink him?
What does Alberto teach that a parent cannot?
activity: Each person names one 'land' thing they want to try that feels a bit sea-monster scary. Plan one small first step.
parent: Works as a friendship movie first. If you want the identity metaphor, let the child lead; do not force a coming-out reading.
content: Parental fear, a chase, mild bullying. Warm overall.

title: Fly Away Home
learn: Imprinting, migration, father-daughter repair through a shared project
knowledge: Canada geese migration, ultralight aircraft, habitat disruption
questions: Why can't the geese just 'figure out' south without help?
What is Amy practicing besides flying?
When does a parent need to follow a child's lead on a project?
activity: Trace a real migratory route on a map. Estimate days and hazards. Compare to the film.
parent: Opens with a car accident and a mother's death. Tell kids beforehand or start after the title sequence if needed.
content: Parental death at the start, flight danger, developers as antagonists. True-story inspired.

title: Mulan
learn: Courage as cleverness, family honor vs. self, wartime gender rules
knowledge: Legendary China setting (story, not textbook history)
questions: What does Mulan save besides China?
When is disguise protection and when is it a prison?
activity: List three problems Mulan solves with brains instead of force.
parent: Use the legend as story, then note it is not a documentary about China.
content: War, a frightening Shan Yu, implied death. G but intense in battle.

title: Turning Red
learn: Puberty as metaphor, mother-daughter control vs. care, friend groups as labs
knowledge: Toronto Chinese-Canadian family life, temple tradition in a modern city
questions: What is Mei's mother afraid will happen if she loosens her grip?
activity: Each person names a 'red panda' — a feeling that arrives too big for the room.
parent: Period talk is frank and healthy. Preview if you want to set family language first.
content: Puberty themes, family yelling, a concert climax. PG.

title: Elemental
learn: Immigration, mixed communities, duty to parents vs. own path
knowledge: City-as-immigrant-story metaphor
questions: What rule in Element City is really a habit of fear?
activity: Cook or buy a food from a culture your family did not grow up in. Learn one story behind it.
parent: Softer than Zootopia; good for younger kids on belonging.
content: Flood peril, family pressure. Gentle.

title: Newsies
learn: Child labor, collective action, newspapers as power
knowledge: 1899 New York newsboy strike (musical version)
questions: What can kids change when adults own the presses?
activity: Write a one-page 'extra' about a fairness issue at school. Headline required.
parent: Musical, not documentary. Pair with a short real-strike paragraph after.
content: Street hardship, strike violence at a distance. PG.

title: Stand and Deliver
learn: Calculus as access, stereotype threat, teacher as organizer
knowledge: AP calculus, East L.A. in the 1980s, testing politics
questions: Why do the students have to prove the scores twice?
activity: Work one hard problem together until everyone can explain one step.
parent: Talky and dated in style; the fairness ending still lands.
content: Language, teen pregnancy subplot, class conflict. 12+.

title: Little Women
learn: Art vs. money, sisterhood, 19th-century limits on girls
knowledge: Civil War home front, publishing, women's economic options then
questions: Which March sister is choosing freedom, and which is choosing safety?
activity: Write two versions of the same page: one 'for the market,' one 'for yourself.'
parent: Gerwig structure jumps in time — help younger viewers once, then let it play.
content: Illness and death, poverty stress. PG.

title: School of Rock
learn: Ensemble music, finding a role, adults who are still unfinished
knowledge: Rock band roles; school as institution vs. workshop
questions: What does each kid bring that Dewey did not plan for?
activity: Form a 20-minute living-room band with pots, playlists, or real instruments. Assign jobs.
parent: PG-13 for language and a fake-teacher plot you should label as comedy, not advice.
content: Deceit premise, rock lyrics, mild language. Fun with a disclaimer.

title: Night at the Museum
learn: Museums as story warehouses, history figures as personalities
knowledge: Natural history museum mash-up (starter, not accurate syllabus)
questions: Which exhibit would you want to talk to, and what would you ask?
activity: Pick one real object from a museum site. Write five true facts vs. five movie inventions.
parent: Gateway film. Follow with a real visit or virtual tour so magic does not replace history.
content: Comic chase action. Easy.

title: Charlotte's Web
learn: Friendship across difference, words that change fate, farm life cycles
knowledge: Farm seasons; how stories travel
questions: What does Charlotte give Wilbur that bacon economics cannot?
activity: Write three words that would save someone — specific, true, short.
parent: Death is quiet and clear. Stay for it. The book still outruns the film if they want more.
content: Animal death handled gently.

title: The King's Speech
learn: Speech work, friendship across class, leadership as practice
knowledge: Abdication crisis, radio as mass medium, WWII prelude
questions: Why does Bertie need a friend more than a speech coach?
activity: Read a paragraph aloud twice: once rushed, once after three slow breaths.
parent: Rated R mainly for coaching-session language. If that is a no, skip. Historically rich for 13+.
content: Strong language in therapy scenes; stuttering depicted in depth. R.

title: The Pursuit of Happyness
learn: Unstable housing, unpaid internships as a gamble, fathering under scarcity
knowledge: 1980s Bay Area finance intern culture; homelessness
questions: What systems fail Chris besides 'not trying hard enough'?
activity: Map a monthly budget with rent as the first line. What disappears when rent doubles?
parent: Inspiring and stressful. Do not use as a simple bootstrap fable; name the luck and the grind.
content: Homelessness, brief violence, language. PG-13. Heavy.

title: Gifted
learn: Giftedness vs. a whole childhood, who owns a child's mind
knowledge: Mathematics culture, custody as values fight
questions: What does Mary need besides harder problems?
activity: Learn one elegant idea (infinity hotel, primes) and explain it to someone younger.
parent: Courtroom plus grief. Better for tweens than the trailer suggests.
content: Language, adult conflict, a mother's suicide in backstory. PG-13.

title: Spirited Away
learn: Work as identity, greed, keeping your name
knowledge: Bathhouse folklore, Japanese spirit world imagery
questions: What happens when Chihiro stops acting like a guest and starts acting like a worker?
activity: List every job Chihiro does. Which one changes her most?
parent: Dense and strange on purpose. Reassure younger watchers that the parents return.
content: Transformation body horror-lite, eerie spirits. PG with real unease.

title: Up
learn: Grief, adventure late in life, promises that need updating
knowledge: Exploration history as personal myth
questions: What adventure was Carl missing that was already in the house?
activity: Make a 'married life' style page of your year in six silent images.
parent: Opening montage is famous and devastating. Preview for sensitive kids.
content: Death of a spouse, mild peril. PG.

title: Paddington
learn: Immigration welcome, manners, found family
knowledge: London as arrival city
questions: What does 'please look after this bear' ask of a whole city?
activity: Write a welcome card for a new student that includes one useful local tip.
parent: Start here if 2 feels like a sequel jump. 2 is stronger; 1 teaches the welcome.
content: Comic villain, mild danger. Very safe.

title: How to Train Your Dragon 2
learn: Leadership after loss, war ethics with animals
knowledge: Sequel-level politics of dragon riding
questions: What kind of leader does Hiccup refuse to become?
activity: Compare Hiccup's method to Drago's in a two-column chart.
parent: Contains a major parental death. Do not surprise families who loved the first film.
content: War action, death of a parent. Heavier than film 1.
